claims.text: The starting HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of 786 MPa.
The starting HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The starting HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static fracture strain of 13.5%.
Post-cold-work subcritical annealing can be tuned to produce fine recrystallized grains embedded in a coarse deformed matrix in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Fine-grained regions in the proposed bimodal structure will increase dislocation storage and back-stress.
Fine-grained regions will introduce additional barriers to dislocation motion and thereby enhance dynamic strain hardening.
Retained coarse deformed grains will preserve ductility in the treated alloy.
A bimodal microstructure can provide a favorable combination of strength and ductility.
Improved strain hardenability suppresses or delays shear localization under dynamic loading.
Thermal softening during adiabatic shear-band formation can cause premature failure.
The treatment will increase the dynamic yield strength of HfZrTiTa0.53 by approximately 200 MPa or more relative to the stated quasi-static baseline.
The treatment will improve uniform deformation before localization under high-rate loading.
The treatment will delay adiabatic shear-band formation in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The treatment will produce a more gradual impact-induced energy-release profile.
The predictions apply to adiabatic, impact-like loading at room temperature and strain rates of 10^3 to 10^4 s^-1.
SHPB testing and microscopy can be used to compare dynamic stress-strain response and adiabatic shear localization between baseline and treated specimens.

contradictions.description: The prediction is phrased as a comparison of dynamically loaded treated material with quasi-static baseline properties, whereas the falsification experiment compares treated and untreated specimens both tested dynamically. These are different comparators, so the stated 200 MPa improvement relative to 786 MPa is not directly tested by the matched experiment.
